newsitem.title: FRANCE: French hauliers protest Spanish truckers violence.
newsitem.headline: French hauliers protest Spanish truckers violence.

text.p: French road hauliers denounced striking Spanish truckers on Friday and blamed an atmosphere of violence "close to insurrection" for the death of a Spanish picket run over by a French trucker.
They said they would insist that French companies whose trucks are stranded get compensation.
France has now barred trucks from driving into north-west Spain and the French envoy in Madrid has asked Spanish authorities to ensure the protection of stranded French truckers.
"However legitimate their demands, the squads of strikers and the aggressive atmosphere they generate can only be condemned," the French Road Haulage Federation said in a statement.

About 50 French truckers were stranded by the week-old strike and faced attacks both against themselves and their vehicles, the federation said. "Such violence no longer has anything to do with a strike."
It said it was taking steps to ensure that French transport companies were compensated for losses.

Joel Sereira, the 21-year-old trucker who drove through a strikers' roadblock in Thursday's fatal clash, was released on bail. He told French television he panicked when four pickets stoned his truck. "It was pure fear. I believed they were going to kill me," he said.
He said he first believed he had run over a piece of timber then realised it was one of the pickets. "I did not intend to kill him. I am not a murderer," he said.
He has been released on bail and the federation said he was under the protection of the French consulate and would travel to France, or Portugal where he has relatives.
In a re-play of the French truckers' strike last year which disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding a revamp of their sector.
In addition to reducing the retirement age to 60 years from 65, drivers are pushing for diesel subsidies, a revision of tariffs and recognition of work-rated illnesses.
French truck drivers won a number of concessions last year, including wage rises and retirement at 55 instead of 60.
